$comment: A second family tree, orthogonal to bedrock.json's composition tree. Composition asks 'what is X made of' (organs, cells, molecules — downward into parts). Taxonomy asks 'what IS X' (a classification by shared traits — upward into categories). Every group has exactly one parent: real taxonomic rank is a strict hierarchy, not a DAG like composition can be. Sourced from Wikipedia rather than the school-level PDFs that prompted this file, to match every other fact in this game.

groups.name: Animalia
groups.fact: Multicellular, eukaryotic, and unlike plants or fungi, gets its energy by eating other organisms rather than making its own food.

groups.name: Chordata
groups.fact: Defined by a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, and paired pharyngeal slits — all present at some point in development, even in species where the adult loses them.

groups.name: Vertebrata
groups.fact: The notochord present in every chordate embryo is replaced, in this group alone, by a bony or cartilaginous vertebral column by adulthood.

groups.name: Mammalia
groups.fact: Warm-blooded, has hair or fur at some life stage, and the females produce milk from mammary glands — the trait that gives the class its name.

groups.name: Aves
groups.fact: The only living animals with feathers. Warm-blooded, lays hard-shelled eggs, and its forelimbs are modified into wings even in flightless species.

groups.name: Reptilia
groups.fact: Cold-blooded, breathes with lungs, and covered in dry, scaly skin rather than the moist skin of an amphibian. Most lay leathery or hard-shelled eggs on land.

groups.name: Amphibia
groups.fact: Cold-blooded with smooth, permeable skin used for extra gas exchange — most start life in water breathing through gills and move onto land as lungs develop.

groups.name: Ray-finned fish
groups.fact: Fins supported by bony spines (rays) rather than the fleshy lobes of a lungfish or the cartilage of a shark — about 96% of all living fish species belong here.

groups.name: Cartilaginous fish
groups.fact: A skeleton built entirely of cartilage rather than bone — sharks, rays and skates all belong here, one of the oldest still-living vertebrate lineages.

groups.name: Arthropoda
groups.fact: A segmented body in a jointed exoskeleton, which has to be moulted to grow — the largest animal phylum by far, over 80% of all described animal species.

groups.name: Insecta
groups.fact: A body in three parts — head, thorax, abdomen — six jointed legs, and usually two antennae. More described species than every other animal class combined.

groups.name: Arachnida
groups.fact: Eight legs and no antennae, unlike an insect's six legs and two antennae. Spiders, scorpions, ticks and mites all belong here.

groups.name: Malacostraca
groups.fact: The largest class of crustaceans — crabs, lobsters, shrimp and woodlice — typically with a body in a head, thorax and abdomen, and paired appendages on most segments.

groups.name: Mollusca
groups.fact: Soft-bodied, usually with a muscular foot and a mantle that in most species secretes a shell — the second-largest animal phylum after arthropods.

groups.name: Gastropoda
groups.fact: Snails and slugs — molluscs that move on a single broad foot, most with a coiled shell, though slugs have reduced or lost theirs entirely.

groups.name: Cephalopoda
groups.fact: Octopuses, squid and cuttlefish — the foot is drawn up around the head into arms or tentacles, and this is the most intelligent class of invertebrate known.

groups.name: Bivalvia
groups.fact: Mussels, oysters, clams and scallops — a shell in two hinged halves and no radula, the rasping tongue almost every other mollusc feeds with.

groups.name: Cnidaria
groups.fact: Radially symmetric, with stinging cells called cnidocytes on its tentacles — jellyfish, corals and sea anemones all belong here.

groups.name: Echinodermata
groups.fact: Exclusively marine, with a calcium-carbonate skeleton just under the skin and a water-driven vascular system used for movement — starfish, sea urchins, sea cucumbers.

groups.name: Annelida
groups.fact: Segmented worms — earthworms, leeches, ragworms — the body divided into repeating rings, each usually carrying its own set of internal organs.

groups.name: Platyhelminthes
groups.fact: Flatworms — soft, unsegmented, with no body cavity and a gut (where present) with only one opening, serving as both mouth and anus.

groups.name: Porifera
groups.fact: Sponges — no true tissues, nerves or organs, just a loose aggregate of specialised cells filtering food from water pumped through the body's own pores.

groups.name: Primates
groups.fact: Forward-facing eyes for depth perception, a large brain relative to body size, and grasping hands — includes lemurs, monkeys, apes, and humans.

groups.name: Carnivora
groups.fact: Named for a shared ancestor's diet, not every member's — pandas and some other carnivorans eat mostly plants — but nearly all keep the order's blade-like carnassial teeth.

groups.name: Cetacea
groups.fact: Whales, dolphins and porpoises — mammals that returned to full-time ocean life, breathing air through a blowhole and giving birth to live young underwater.

groups.name: Artiodactyla
groups.fact: Even-toed hoofed mammals — cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, camels, deer and giraffes — weight-bearing carried on the third and fourth toes equally.

groups.name: Perissodactyla
groups.fact: Odd-toed hoofed mammals — horses, zebras, donkeys, and rhinoceroses — weight carried mainly on a single central toe.

groups.name: Rodentia
groups.fact: A single pair of ever-growing incisors in each jaw, worn down by constant gnawing — the largest order of mammals, over 40% of all mammal species.

groups.name: Lagomorpha
groups.fact: Rabbits, hares and pikas — often mistaken for rodents, but with an extra, tiny pair of upper incisors set behind the main pair, which rodents lack.

groups.name: Squamata
groups.fact: Lizards and snakes — the largest reptile order, unified by skin covered in overlapping horny scales and, in most, a lower jaw loosely hinged for a wide gape.

groups.name: Testudines
groups.fact: Turtles and tortoises — a bony shell fused to the spine and ribs, unique among vertebrates, with the shoulder and hip girdles inside the rib cage rather than outside it.

groups.name: Galliformes
groups.fact: Heavy-bodied, mostly ground-feeding birds — chickens, turkeys, pheasants, quail — strong legs built for scratching at the ground rather than sustained flight.

groups.name: Anseriformes
groups.fact: Waterfowl — ducks, geese and swans — webbed feet and a broad, flattened bill often edged with comb-like lamellae for filtering food from water.

groups.name: Hymenoptera
groups.fact: Bees, wasps and ants — two pairs of membranous wings linked by tiny hooks so they beat as one, and among the most social insects in the animal kingdom.

groups.name: Lepidoptera
groups.fact: Butterflies and moths — wings covered in tiny overlapping scales, which is where the order's name comes from: Greek for 'scale wing'.

groups.name: Nematoda
groups.fact: Roundworms — an unsegmented, tubular body with a fluid-filled pseudocoelom. The most numerous animal phylum by individual count; most species are free-living, but some, like Ascaris, are parasites.

groups.name: Proboscidea
groups.fact: Elephants and their extinct relatives — the only living mammal order defined by a trunk, a fusion of the nose and upper lip used for breathing, feeding, and grasping.

groups.name: Diprotodontia
groups.fact: The largest order of marsupials — kangaroos, koalas, wombats and possums — named for their two large, forward-pointing lower incisors.

groups.name: Monotremata
groups.fact: The only mammal order that lays eggs rather than giving live birth — just the platypus and four echidna species survive today.

groups.name: Lamniformes
groups.fact: Mackerel sharks — just 15 living species in 8 families, but among them the great white, the makos, the threshers, the basking shark and the goblin shark. Two of those families keep parts of their body warmer than the surrounding sea.

groups.name: Carcharhiniformes
groups.fact: Ground sharks — over 270 species, the largest shark order by far, spanning catsharks, requiem sharks and hammerheads. Nearly every member carries a nictitating membrane that draws over the eye to protect it during an attack.

groups.name: Myliobatiformes
groups.fact: Stingrays and their relatives — eagle rays, cownose rays and manta rays among them. Most carry one or more venomous barbed spines at the base of the tail; the mantas are the exception, having lost the spine entirely.

groups.name: Octopoda
groups.fact: About 300 species, all eight-armed and, since their coleoid ancestors internalised it, entirely without a shell — internal or external.

groups.name: Vampyromorphida
groups.fact: A single living species, Vampyroteuthis infernalis. Molecular studies place it as the sister group to octopuses, diverging before true squid and octopuses split.

groups.name: Oegopsida
groups.fact: Open-eyed squid — the eye has no corneal covering at all. One of several orders 'Teuthida' used to lump together before that grouping was abandoned; giant squid belongs here.

groups.name: Nautilida
groups.fact: A once-diverse order reduced to a single family today, Nautilidae — the only living cephalopods that still carry an external shell.

groups.name: Anthozoa
groups.fact: Corals, sea anemones and their relatives — every one of them spends its whole life as a polyp. No cnidarian in this group ever has a free-swimming medusa stage.

groups.name: Hexacorallia
groups.fact: Anthozoans built on six-fold symmetry — stony reef-building corals and sea anemones both belong here, against the eight-fold symmetry of the soft corals in Octocorallia.

groups.name: Actiniaria
groups.fact: True sea anemones — solitary polyps with no skeleton at all, holding their shape with a hydrostatic skeleton of fluid instead.

groups.name: Medusozoa
groups.fact: Cnidarians whose life cycle includes a free-swimming medusa stage — the bell-and-tentacles body plan most people picture when they hear 'jellyfish'.

groups.name: Scyphozoa
groups.fact: The 'true' jellyfish. A single sessile polyp buds off a stack of young medusae, one at a time, in a process called strobilation.

groups.name: Cubozoa
groups.fact: Box jellyfish were classed as an order of Scyphozoa until 1973, when their own life cycle and their true, lensed eyes earned them a class of their own.

groups.name: Hydrozoa
groups.fact: The most varied cnidarian class — solitary hydroids and colonial siphonophores both belong here, most alternating between a polyp stage and a medusa stage.

groups.name: Siphonophorae
groups.fact: Colonies built from specialised zooids that bud from one fertilised egg and stay fused — no single member could survive alone, but the colony functions as one animal.

groups.name: Asteroidea
groups.fact: Starfish — about 1,900 species, moving on a hydraulic water-vascular system of fluid-filled canals, and many able to regrow an entire lost arm.

groups.name: Orectolobiformes
groups.fact: Carpet sharks — around 43 species in 7 families, with a small mouth that never extends past the eyes and, in most species, a pair of sensory barbels beside the nostrils. Bottom-dwelling nurse and wobbegong sharks belong here, and so does the whale shark, the largest fish alive.

groups.name: Lophiiformes
groups.fact: Anglerfishes — about 13 families united by the illicium, a modified fin ray tipped with a lure called the esca that draws prey close. In deep-sea species the esca glows, lit by colonies of symbiotic bioluminescent bacteria.

groups.name: Perciformes
groups.fact: Once defined so broadly it held around 41% of all bony fish species, until molecular studies split most of that apart. What's left has since absorbed the former orders Scorpaeniformes and Gasterosteiformes, so groupers, lionfish and stonefish now classify here too, alongside perches and basses.

groups.name: Felidae
groups.fact: Retractile claws and carnassial teeth built for tearing and cutting flesh — every one of the 41 living species is an obligate carnivore, meat is not optional.

groups.name: Pantherinae
groups.fact: The 'big cat' subfamily — five Panthera species plus the two clouded leopards — split from the rest of Felidae in the Miocene, roughly 6 to 10 million years ago.

groups.name: Machairodontinae
groups.fact: The sabertooth cats — elongated upper canines, the earliest-diverging branch of the whole cat family, and gone since the end-Pleistocene extinction with no living descendants.

groups.name: Panthera
groups.fact: Tiger, lion, jaguar, leopard and snow leopard — unified by an incompletely ossified hyoid bone and an elastic-padded larynx that lets every member roar, except the snow leopard.

groups.name: Canidae
groups.fact: Long legs and a lithe body built for chasing prey, non-retractable claws, and carnassial teeth shaped for shearing flesh — around 37 living species, from the 24 cm fennec fox to the gray wolf.

groups.name: Canis
groups.fact: Wolves, coyotes, jackals and the domestic dog — every species here has 78 chromosomes and can potentially interbreed with every other.

groups.name: Canis lupus
groups.fact: One species holding the gray wolf and every domestic dog breed alike — Canis lupus familiaris is formally a subspecies of the wolf, not a separate species, and the dingo is another.

groups.name: Gadiformes
groups.fact: Cod, hake, haddock and their relatives — nearly all marine, mostly cold-water, with pelvic fins set below or ahead of the pectorals. Many are major commercial food fish; the burbot is the order's only fully freshwater member.

groups.name: Clupeiformes
groups.fact: Herring, sardines, anchovies and shad — silvery, spindle-shaped schooling fish that make up many of the ocean's most important forage species, feeding an enormous share of everything above them in the food web.

groups.name: Salmoniformes
groups.fact: Salmon and trout in one suborder, pike and mudminnows in the other — two lineages closely enough related to sit in a single order, united by a small rayless adipose fin between the dorsal fin and the tail.

groups.name: Cypriniformes
groups.fact: Carp, goldfish, koi, minnows and loaches — over 4,200 species with no teeth in the jaw at all; instead they grind food with pharyngeal teeth in the throat, working against a pad at the base of the skull.

groups.name: Anguilliformes
groups.fact: True eels — about 1,000 species with no pelvic fins, dorsal and anal fins fused into a single ribbon running most of the body's length, and a flat, transparent larval stage called a leptocephalus found in no other fish order.

groups.name: Siluriformes
groups.fact: Catfish — roughly one in twenty of all vertebrate species alive, none of them scaled, most named for the whisker-like barbels around the mouth that smell and feel for food in murky water.

groups.name: Carangiformes
groups.fact: Once just the jacks and trevallies, this order has absorbed a wide swath of the old Perciformes as genetic studies reorganised the bony-fish tree — jacks, barracudas, remoras, flatfishes, swordfish and marlin now all classify here together.

groups.name: Syngnathiformes
groups.fact: Seahorses, pipefish and their relatives — a tubular, toothless snout that sucks in prey at close range, and in most species the male, not the female, carries the fertilised eggs to term.

groups.name: Blenniiformes
groups.fact: Blennies and damselfish — including the anemonefish — sat scattered across the old order Perciformes until genetic studies showed they form their own lineage; Eschmeyer's Catalog of Fishes now groups them here instead.

groups.name: Characiformes
groups.fact: Piranhas and tetras share this order's defining feature, a Weberian apparatus — a chain of small bones linking the swim bladder to the inner ear, sharpening hearing in fresh water.

groups.name: Centrarchiformes
groups.fact: North American sunfish and bass on one branch, Australian grunters and hawkfishes on another — recently split out of Perciformes, and still missing from some textbooks even as fish databases now accept it.

groups.name: Coleoptera
groups.fact: Beetles — the largest insect order by far, with more described species than any other order in the animal kingdom. Defined by a hardened pair of forewings, elytra, that meet in a straight line down the back and cover the flight wings beneath.

groups.name: Odonata
groups.fact: Dragonflies and damselflies — one of the oldest still-living insect lineages, with a fossil record going back over 300 million years, long before dinosaurs.

groups.name: Orthoptera
groups.fact: Grasshoppers, crickets and locusts — powerful hind legs built for jumping, and in most species, sound produced by rubbing one body part against another.

groups.name: Mantodea
groups.fact: Praying mantises — an elongated thorax and a pair of spiked, grasping forelegs held folded in front of the body, ready to snap out at passing prey.

groups.name: Blattodea
groups.fact: Cockroaches, and, nested inside them as their closest living relatives, termites — a group united by molecular evidence more than by looks.

groups.name: Siphonaptera
groups.fact: Fleas — wingless, laterally flattened, and built almost entirely around one skill: jumping onto a passing host to feed on its blood.

groups.name: Araneae
groups.fact: Spiders — every one of the roughly 50,000 described species has silk-producing spinnerets and fanged chelicerae, though not every species spins a web to catch prey.

groups.name: Scorpiones
groups.fact: Scorpions — a pair of grasping pedipalps and a narrow, segmented tail ending in a venomous stinger, the telson. Unusually among arachnids, every species gives birth to live young.

groups.name: Ixodida
groups.fact: Ticks — obligate blood-feeders at every stage past the egg, and the primary route by which diseases like Lyme disease pass from wildlife into people.

groups.name: Chilopoda
groups.fact: Centipedes — fast, venomous predators with exactly one pair of legs per body segment, injected through forcipules, a modified front pair of legs rather than fangs.

groups.name: Diplopoda
groups.fact: Millipedes — slow-moving detritivores with two pairs of legs per body segment, twice a centipede's count, and no species with anywhere near 1,000 legs.

groups.name: Isopoda
groups.fact: Isopods — seven pairs of walking legs and a body of overlapping plates. Most are marine, but the woodlice of suborder Oniscidea are the only crustaceans to have fully adapted to life on dry land.

groups.name: Dinosauria
groups.fact: Defined by hip and hindlimb traits that hold the body upright, off to the side, rather than sprawled like a lizard's — includes every dinosaur that ever lived, and, since birds are its one surviving lineage, still does.

groups.name: Saurischia
groups.fact: The 'lizard-hipped' dinosaurs, named for a pubis bone pointed forward as in a lizard — an ironic name, since this is the saurischian line, not the 'bird-hipped' Ornithischia, that actually gave rise to birds.

groups.name: Ornithischia
groups.fact: The 'bird-hipped' dinosaurs, named for a backward-pointed pubis bone that happens to resemble a bird's — despite the name, every living bird actually descends from the other dinosaur lineage, Saurischia.

groups.name: Theropoda
groups.fact: Bipedal, mostly meat-eating dinosaurs, hollow-boned and three-toed — and the only dinosaur lineage with living members, since every bird alive today is technically a theropod.

groups.name: Sauropodomorpha
groups.fact: Long-necked, small-headed herbivorous dinosaurs, running from early bipedal forms through the four-legged giants of Sauropoda — the largest land animals that have ever lived.

groups.name: Thyreophora
groups.fact: Armoured herbivorous dinosaurs, defined as everything closer to Ankylosaurus and Stegosaurus than to Iguanodon or Triceratops — rows of bony plates or spikes set into the skin distinguish the group across 130 million years.

groups.name: Marginocephalia
groups.fact: Herbivorous dinosaurs sharing a bony shelf or margin at the back of the skull — in ceratopsians it flares into a frill, in pachycephalosaurs it thickens into a dome.

groups.name: Ornithopoda
groups.fact: Beaked, mostly bipedal-capable herbivorous dinosaurs with increasingly sophisticated batteries of grinding teeth — the line that runs from small early browsers up to the duck-billed hadrosaurs.

groups.name: Coelurosauria
groups.fact: Every theropod closer to birds than to Allosaurus — tyrannosaurs, ostrich-mimics, raptors and birds all belong here, and fossil skin impressions show even its earliest members were feathered.

groups.name: Megalosauroidea
groups.fact: A lineage of large-bodied theropods including the spinosaurids — sail- or ridge-backed, often long-snouted predators adapted, in several members, to hunting near or in water.

groups.name: Carnosauria
groups.fact: Large predatory theropods closer to Allosaurus than to living birds — a group that, despite the name's old association with the biggest meat-eaters, does not include Tyrannosaurus, which classifies elsewhere, in Coelurosauria.

groups.name: Paraves
groups.fact: Every theropod closer to living birds than to the oviraptorosaurs — split between the sickle-clawed Deinonychosauria and Avialae, the birds themselves. It is the clade where the line between 'dinosaur' and 'bird' gets genuinely hard to draw.

groups.name: Deinonychosauria
groups.fact: The 'raptors' — dromaeosaurids and troodontids — small to mid-sized feathered theropods best known for an enlarged, sickle-shaped claw on the second toe of each foot.

groups.name: Sauropoda
groups.fact: Four-legged, long-necked, long-tailed herbivores with small heads and pillar-like legs — the largest land animals ever to exist, some reaching well over 30 metres long.

groups.name: Stegosauria
groups.fact: Thyreophorans carrying rows of upright plates or spikes down the back and tail rather than the fused armour of their ankylosaur relatives.

groups.name: Ankylosauria
groups.fact: Heavily armoured, low-slung thyreophorans covered in fused bony plates called osteoderms, several with a stiffened, weaponised tail tip.

groups.name: Ceratopsia
groups.fact: Beaked, herbivorous dinosaurs running from small, largely bipedal early forms to the massive horned, frilled quadrupeds of the Late Cretaceous.

groups.name: Pachycephalosauria
groups.fact: Thick-skulled, mostly bipedal herbivores whose skull roof thickened, in some species, into a solid dome believed to have been used in head-to-head combat.

groups.name: Iguanodontia
groups.fact: Beaked ornithopods running from Iguanodon-grade forms up through the duck-billed hadrosaurs nested inside it — what were once called separate 'iguanodontid' families are now understood as steps along one continuous lineage.

groups.name: Tyrannosauridae
groups.fact: Large-bodied coelurosaurs with deep, massive skulls, tiny two-fingered forelimbs and bone-crushing bite force — Tyrannosaurus is the largest and last-surviving member.

groups.name: Compsognathidae
groups.fact: Small, lightly built coelurosaurs, among them some of the smallest dinosaurs known — Compsognathus itself once held that record.

groups.name: Brachiosauridae
groups.fact: Sauropods with forelimbs longer than their hindlimbs, tilting the body into a steep, giraffe-like incline built for browsing well above the heads of other sauropods.

groups.name: Diplodocidae
groups.fact: Extremely long, whip-tailed sauropods with comparatively slender builds and squared, peg-toothed snouts suited to stripping low vegetation — Apatosaurus and Diplodocus both belong here.

groups.name: Protoceratopsidae
groups.fact: Small, mostly hornless early ceratopsians with a bony frill already present but not yet the huge horns of their later ceratopsid cousins — a real side-branch of the family, not a direct ancestor of them.

groups.name: Ceratopsidae
groups.fact: The large, quadrupedal, horned ceratopsians of the Late Cretaceous — Triceratops among them — carrying the group's biggest horns and most elaborate frills.

groups.name: Hadrosauridae
groups.fact: The 'duck-billed dinosaurs' — the most derived branch of Iguanodontia, with broad, toothless beaks backed by hundreds of grinding teeth, and in several lineages, elaborate hollow head crests.

groups.name: Pterosauria
groups.fact: Flying reptiles that shared the Mesozoic skies with the dinosaurs below them — close archosaur relatives of Dinosauria, but not dinosaurs themselves; wings formed from a skin membrane stretched to a hugely elongated fourth finger.

groups.name: Azhdarchidae
groups.fact: Large to enormous late Cretaceous pterosaurs with long, stiffened necks and long jaws — the group that includes Quetzalcoatlus, a leading contender for the largest flying animal ever known.

groups.name: Plesiosauria
groups.fact: Marine reptiles with four flipper-like limbs, found from the Early Jurassic to the end of the Cretaceous — swimming alongside the dinosaurs, in the same seas, but no closer to them than any other reptile group.

groups.name: Elasmosauridae
groups.fact: Plesiosaurs with the most extreme necks in the group, built from as many as 70 or more vertebrae — Elasmosaurus itself carried 72, among the highest counts known.
